question: Explain the doctrine of Res Sub-Judice under the CPC and state its essential conditions.
gold_answer: ​ Answer Details: Section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, governs the stay of suits (Res Sub-Judice). It prohibits a court from proceeding with the trial of any suit in which the matter in issue is also directly and substantially in issue in a previously instituted suit between the same parties. ​ Essential Conditions: 1.​ There must be two suits (one previously instituted, one subsequently instituted). 2.​ The matter in issue in both suits must be identical. 3.​ The suits must be between the same parties or their litigating representatives. 4.​ The court where the previous suit is pending must have jurisdiction to grant the relief claimed. 5.​ Both parties must be litigating under the same title.
system_answer:
**What This Means For You**
The doctrine of Res Sub-Judice is a legal principle that prevents a court from hearing a case that is already pending in another court. This means that if you have a case pending in one court, you cannot file the same case in another court. This principle is important to prevent multiple courts from hearing the same case and to avoid conflicting decisions.

**What the Law Says**
Under Section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) [ACT-1], a court will not proceed with a suit if the matter is already pending in another court. This is known as the doctrine of Res Sub-Judice. The essential conditions for this doctrine to apply are: (1) the matter must be directly and substantially in issue in both proceedings, (2) the parties in both proceedings must be the same or privies to each other, and (3) the court in which the previous suit is pending must be competent to grant the relief claimed.

**What You Should Do Now**
1. Check if you have any pending cases in other courts related to the same matter.
2. Verify if the parties involved in the new case are the same as those in the pending case.
3. Ensure that the court where the previous case is pending has the jurisdiction to grant the relief you are seeking.

**Evidence to Keep**
- Copies of the pending case documents
- Proof of the parties involved in both cases
- Documents showing the jurisdiction of the court where the previous case is pending

question: What is the distinction between Res Judicata (Section 11) and Constructive Res Judicata?
gold_answer: ​ Answer Details: Section 11 bars a court from trying any suit or issue where the matter has already been directly and substantially decided in a former suit between the same parties by a competent court. ​ Constructive Res Judicata: Found in Explanation IV of Section 11, it states that any matter which might and ought to have been made a ground of defense or attack in such former suit shall be deemed to have been a matter directly and substantially in issue in such suit. If a party fails to raise a claim/defense when they had the chance, they are barred from raising it in subsequent litigation.

The concepts of Res Judicata and Constructive Res Judicata are crucial in understanding how courts handle repeated lawsuits on the same issue. Res Judicata prevents a matter that has already been decided by a competent court from being tried again, while Constructive Res Judicata extends this principle to matters that could have been raised in the previous lawsuit but were not. This distinction is important for individuals to avoid repeated legal battles on the same issue.

**What the Law Says**
Under Section 11 [ACT-1] of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Res Judicata means that no court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties. Constructive Res Judicata, on the other hand, is based on the principle that any matter which might and ought to have been made ground of defence or attack in such former suit shall be deemed to have been a matter directly and substantially in issue in such suit, as explained in Explanation IV of Section 11 [ACT-1]. This means that even if a particular issue was not explicitly decided in the previous lawsuit, if it could have been raised, it is considered to be part of the Res Judicata.

question: Define 'Proposal' and 'Acceptance' and explain when communication becomes complete under the Contract Act.
gold_answer: ​ Answer Details: Section 2(a) defines a proposal (offer) as when one person signifies to another his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other. Section 2(b) states that when the proposal is signified, it is deemed accepted. ​ Completion of Communication (Section 4): ○​ The communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made. ○​ The communication of an acceptance is complete: as against the proposer, when it is put in a course of transmission to him so as to be out of the power of the acceptor; as against the acceptor, when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer.

According to Section 3 of the Contract Act, 1872 [ACT-2], the communication of proposals, acceptances, and revocations can be made by any act or omission that intends to communicate such or has the effect of communicating it.
